questions.q: According to this lesson, what is the actual failure mode that causes good documentation to go stale?
options: Documentation lives somewhere disconnected from the system it describes, so nothing reminds anyone to update it when the system changes
ADRs are inherently too short to capture any useful information
Markdown files cannot be stored in version control
Teams write ADRs that are factually wrong from the start
questions.explain: The ADRs and diagrams from the earlier lessons can be well written and still rot, because documentation stored separately from the infrastructure it describes has nothing forcing it to update when that infrastructure changes.

questions.q: What does co-locating a docs/adr/ directory inside the same repository as the Terraform and Bicep code (from Chapter 2) actually provide?
options: It makes the Terraform plan run faster
It removes the need for a Decision section in any ADR
It is required by the Terraform Registry for provider publishing
ADRs get versioned in the same git history as the code, and a PR touching the infrastructure can be required to reference the relevant ADR in the same diff
questions.explain: Co-location means you can check out any past commit and see which decisions were in force then, and a PR changing infrastructure can be required to touch or reference the matching ADR, making the decision-to-implementation link visible at review time.

questions.q: Why does this lesson prefer review triggers tied to the size and kind of a change over a quarterly calendar reminder?
options: Calendar reminders are technically impossible to set up in most version control systems
Quarterly reviews are banned by most compliance frameworks
A calendar reminder is the first thing a busy team skips, while a trigger tied to the change itself keeps pace with a system that changes every week
Change-triggered reviews require no human reviewer at all
questions.explain: A calendar-based review is easy for a busy team to skip, and that team is exactly the one whose documentation most needs attention -- a trigger tied to the actual change (e.g. a PR checklist item for network/ or landing-zone/) keeps up automatically.

questions.q: In the ADR status lifecycle described in this lesson, what does "Superseded by ADR-00XX" mean?
options: The ADR was deleted and no longer exists in the repository
The decision was replaced by a specific later ADR, and both records are kept and cross-linked
The ADR failed a security scan and must be rewritten
The decision is still in force and unchanged
questions.explain: Superseded means a specific later decision has replaced this one; the old ADR stays in the repository, cross-linked to the new one, so the full history remains readable.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say deleting an outdated ADR is worse than marking it Superseded or Deprecated?
options: Deleting a file from git is technically impossible
It would recreate the oral-history problem from earlier in the chapter -- a later engineer who finds a reference to the old ADR would have nothing left to actually read
Deleted files automatically break the Terraform state file
git forbids removing Markdown files from a repository
questions.explain: Deleting the old record removes the exact context the chapter opened by arguing for -- superseding it instead keeps both the original reasoning and its replacement readable to anyone who finds a reference to it later.
